summary:
San Juan province stands under Argentina's national legal framework, and no San Juan-specific source in the available inventory shows a deviation material enough to score separately. The province is therefore assessed at the national position.

Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012, and promulgated on 24 May 2012, remains formally in force. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and Argentine identity documents have carried an "X" marker since 2021. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010, and the United Nations described the 2012 statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

The framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. Decree DNU 62/2025, published on 5 February 2025 under President Javier Milei, amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law to bar under-18s from gender-affirming surgical and hormonal interventions. A second decree, DNU 61/2025, altered prison-sentencing law to change the placement of trans detainees. Both decrees apply nationally, to every province, and therefore bind San Juan.

Trans activists interviewed by the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 described a chaotic and desperate situation under the Milei government and reported that the 2012 law, while formally in force, is no longer guaranteed in practice. Legal experts and LGBTIQ+ organisations called both decrees unconstitutional, argued that abruptly suspending adolescent treatments endangers trans youth, and filed a judicial challenge.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a figure averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the data on 19 March 2026.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. As the case now stands, the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply.

Activists told the Washington Blade that the government eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, an institutional loss they associated with reduced protection and visibility for trans people at federal level.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration.
localsOnly:
Trans people resident in San Juan are covered by the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans workers. Activists reported in April 2025 that hires made under the quota were dismissed and that the measure is no longer being implemented, an assertion that rests on their testimony rather than on an official statement.

Residents under 18 lose access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy under DNU 62/2025, which amended Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law with effect from 5 February 2025. Legal experts and LGBTIQ+ organisations contended that suspending adolescent treatment abruptly endangers trans youth.

Trans detainees in San Juan prisons are subject to the placement rules changed by DNU 61/2025, which amended prison-sentencing law. Decrees DNU 61/2025 and DNU 62/2025 were both challenged in court as unconstitutional.

Adult legal gender recognition through the provincial and national registry system remains available without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order under Law 26.743, and the "X" marker has been available on the national identity document since 2021.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the constitutional litigation against DNU 62/2025 and DNU 61/2025 is not recorded in the sources available here; whether a court has upheld, suspended or struck down either decree remains unresolved for this assessment.

No San Juan-specific legislative, judicial or administrative source appears in the inventory, so the absence of a provincial deviation is an absence of evidence rather than a verified finding that San Juan has considered and rejected any change.

Whether the Trans Labor Quota Law is formally repealed or merely unenforced is unresolved; the only account of non-implementation comes from activists interviewed in April 2025, and no official confirmation or denial was available.

The 2025 hate-crime total is national, and no breakdown by province was available, so the share of that violence occurring in or attributable to San Juan is not sourced.
